item.title: How to Build Zane and Killjoy in Silver Age
item.description:

How to Build Zane and Killjoy in Silver Age

Interested in building either of the new heroes from Smash Palace: Chorus of Steel? Karol has you covered!

By Karol Ruszkiewicz

|

Published Oct 30, 2026

|

6 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Two brand-new Silver Age-legal heroes join the ranks with Smash Palace: Chorus of Steel: Zane and Killjoy. They're both Warriors... but with a twist! Zane, Broadly Beloved is Revered, while Killjoy, the Crooked Blade is a Reviled Thief.

These combinations introduce entirely new class and talent pairings to the game, opening up fresh avenues for deckbuilding exploration. While there aren't many direct mechanical links between Warrior and the Revered or Reviled talents, both heroes have interesting abilities that give them a unique identity.

Zane, Broadly Beloved

Zane's greatest strength is... well, his strength. He can wield two two-handed swords, which is already an incredible ability for a Warrior. Weapons dictate a Warrior's strategy and deck construction, so choose wisely!

Let's start with the wager payoffs: Celebrant Broadsword, Zane's signature weapon, and Golden Grail. Both offer solid rewards for winning wagers, and giving your weapon go again is a dream for many Warriors. However, this strategy leaves plenty of agency in your opponent's hands.

Similarly, Zane's hero ability is a double-edged sword, no pun intended. Allowing your opponent to choose when you both draw a card can have a huge impact on the game. I'd recommend exploring this strategy against heroes that rarely want to defend. You'll also want to pack plenty of attack reactions to give yourself more control over whether your weapon attacks hit.

Other weapons offer pure efficiency, with Dawnblade and Talishar, the Lost Prince being the two standout options.

At a baseline, Dawnblade offers a three-power attack for one resource, comparable to other dual-wielding setups like double Cintari Sabers or Hatchets of Body and Mind. That comparison alone highlights the sheer power of Zane's ability.

With a single red Run Through and a blue card, you can present attacks for three and then six damage. That's efficiency even Ira would be jealous of!

From there, you can experiment with other ways to grant go again. Lead with Speed, Hit and Run, and other Warrior staples work incredibly well with a dual-Dawnblade setup. Once you start incorporating Flurry generators like Edict of Steel, or Take the Lead to generate Blade Dance tokens, the possibilities really open up.

Talishar, the Lost Prince offers an alternative against decks looking to end the game quickly. Playing against a Wizard or an aggressive Ninja? Maybe that extra damage is exactly what you need to close things out.

It does come at an additional resource cost, so you'll probably need to adjust your cost curve, but experimenting with different configurations, such as Dawnblade and Talishar or a wager sword alongside Dawnblade, opens up some fascinating deckbuilding possibilities.

Cheers!

What about the Revered side of things?

If stacking Toughness tokens is your thing, you could cosplay as Tuffnut with four intellect and two enormous swords.

Cards like Dig In and Humble Entrance can help fuel powerful, disruptive defensive cards like Disarm and Disperse. They might be a little tricky to line up, but they're interesting options to consider when building your resource base.

The really exciting part of the Revered card pool is the selection of cards that cheer you.

While winning wagers can generate cheers fairly reliably, the ideal time to make both players draw cards is at the very end of your opponent's turn, preferably when they're out of action points and already have a card ready for arsenal.

That's why cards like Helm of the Adored, Shining Courage, and Will of the Crowd offer some of the most compelling cheer synergies.

Aggro or Control?

So how does Zane actually play? Does he lean into aggressive damage output or take a more controlling approach with Toughness tokens?

The beauty of having such a wide card pool is that you can adjust that balance however you like.

Cards like Hit and Run let you build wider combat chains, potentially even making attack-chain finishers viable. Other cards like Snatch, Flock of the Feather Walkers, and Smash Up could also work alongside your weapon attacks.

I'm incredibly curious to see how players approach Zane. He offers something genuinely new to the Warrior class, and I suspect there's plenty of room for experimentation.

Killjoy, the Crooked Blade

Killjoy shines in Ultimate Pit Fight, but when it comes to Silver Age her hero ability and weapon are much more dependent on the metagame–particularly when it comes to stealing Gold. While I expect this hero to excite deckbuilders everywhere, I think her biggest appeal lies in her unique class and talent combination.

Higher Life or Lower Life?

Killjoy's hero ability encourages you to gradually control the game while staying at a lower life total and booing your opponent. However, a decent portion of the Reviled card pool rewards you for having more life than your opponent. Cards like Mocking Blow and Insult to Injury are powerful, but their incentives can clash with Killjoy's ability.

I'd recommend deciding which Reviled synergies you want to prioritize before diving too deeply into deck construction. Trying to maximize both approaches could leave your deck pulling in opposite directions.

Boo!

While getting full value out of Mocking Blow is satisfying, there's something inherently entertaining about making your opponent lose life just because you can. Cards like Horns of the Despised, Villainous Pose, and Concealed Object lean into that fantasy perfectly.

Warrior's Prowess

I could go on and on about the efficiency of cards like Decimator Great Axe, Steel to the Dome and Engage Steel, but the card that really captures the killjoy aspect of this hero is Steelblade Shunt.

Combined with Killjoy's hero ability, Steelblade Shunt opens up an interesting path toward controlling the game and manipulating both heroes' life totals. Playing defensively also gives you more opportunities to trigger her ability, making this a particularly appealing direction for players who enjoy a slower, more reactive style of Warrior.

She's a Thief!

The Thief card pool is still relatively small... for now. But it already offers some incredible counterplay against Gold-based heroes.

If heroes like Olympia, Gravy Bones, and Victor Goldmane start climbing toward the top of the metagame, cards like Light Fingers and Cutpurse Rapier become much more appealing.

And then there's Money or Your Life? That's another fun way to deal some non-physical damage!

Closing Thoughts

If you're an avid brewer like me, you'll already see the world of possibilities these heroes offer. It's not just the combination of Warrior with the Revered and Reviled talents, with a sprinkle of Thief thrown in, but the hero abilities themselves that make Zane and Killjoy so exciting to explore.

They bring something fresh to Silver Age, but if you've never tried multiplayer Flesh and Blood, Smash Palace Warrior is also a great place to start. Not only do you get two fascinating new heroes, but you also get a box full of fun for four players, thanks to the tailor-made event deck.

Whether you're looking to experiment with unconventional Warrior builds or just cause a little chaos around the table, there's plenty to get excited about!

item.title: The Best Decks from Disney Lorcana Challenge Bangkok
item.description:
Disney Lorcana|competitive

The Best Decks from Disney Lorcana Challenge Bangkok

Wait, Detectives are good now?!

By Scott Mines

|@HowlingMines
|

Published Nov 4, 2026

|

12 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

"WHAT?! The Fates are here, and YOU DIDN'T TELL ME?!" 

Ahem, sorry. 

I think the Season of Villainy is awakening something in me. Disney Lorcana's third season of Organized Play has officially begun, overshadowing the holiday season with dastardly laughter and tinkering minions. After all, it feels so good to be bad. 

With this debut, the game has changed in more ways than one. The era of playing for those golden Mickey Mouse - Brave Little Tailor has come to an end. Instead, it's the impressive Hades - Dark Usurper who stands as the ultimate prize. As much as Mickey will always be the first, the alternative variants of Hades really do a lot for me. It's a worthy grail for aspiring players and collectors. 

There's also the introduction of Hyperia City, which has been a confusing affair to watch unfold. The cards within are clearly powerful, and ink drops redefine what's possible on each turn of the game... but there were some seriously unshakeable juggernauts at the top of the format when the set was released. Surely these cards add to those problems more than they provide a reprieve? 

Thankfully, the answer coming out of this weekend's Disney Lorcana Challenge in Bangkok was a resounding "maybe". The kingpins of the format showed up in force with a smattering of new tools, but a handful of newer archetypes also managed a breakout performance that not only puts them on the radar going forward but inspires hope that Hyperia City is far from solved. 

That's exactly the style of event I want to dig into the data for early in a season, so grab yourself a cup o' joe and settle in for a comfy selection of the best decks from Disney Lorcana Challenge Bangkok.

Amber Emerald Circle of Life

It seems apt to kick things off with the villain of the story, doesn't it? 

Amber Emerald was one of the known quantities heading into Bangkok, sitting comfortably as one of the top decks in the format. Despite that, two copies of the deck would meet in the finals to play for all the marbles. 

Fellow content creator Avery from Quest For Two would manage to conquer the event with their traditional spin on the deck, so let us take a closer look at the tools that got it done. 

BloodthirstyAvery's Amber Emerald Circle of Life - 1st Place at Disney Lorcana Challenge Bangkok

Avery's deck was lovingly named "Doing His Part" — in reference to the snazzy piece of tech for the weekend, Aladdin - Doing His Part. None of the other Circle of Life decks in the top sixteen featured any copies of Aladdin, with many further down featuring one or less. The three copies presented here provided a strong hedge against the various Retro Evolution Device decks and happened to come up big against the breakout Ruby Emerald decks built around Rivera Family Photo and The Torn Corner.

This is very much a case of "If it ain't broke, don't fix it" as far as I'm concerned. Avery's list featured exactly two cards from Hyperia City: Don Karnage - Debonair Pirate and Above the Crowd. The former is an exceptionally well-stated threat that both eliminates opposing characters and prevents the opponent from racing, while the latter is just a clean spot removal effect for any problematic glimmer that needs to be shut down on your way to Prince Phillip - Vanquisher of Foes.

Otherwise, the deck hasn't changed much from other recent iterations. Your primary goal is to set up a board of efficient singers that are difficult for the opponent to remove, then leverage them to enable one-sided board wipes that take over a game. At that point, it's fairly trivial to quest out to get over the line. 

The most infamous of these is the pairing of Malicious - Mean and Scary and Circle of Life. If you manage to ditch a Prince Phillip - Vanquisher of Foes with either Tod - Clever Fox or Strike a Good Match, you can sing both songs in the same turn to pile damage into the opposing board and sweep it all away. This isn't too dissimilar to how Under the Sea used to operate in Amber Emerald Dogs — it just takes the game away. 

If you need something a little faster, you can rely on the package of Malicious, Mean and Scary, To Wither a Flower and Max Goof - Rebellious Teen instead. If you can establish a character with Singer 4, you can hardcast Malicious, Mean and Scary before singing To Wither a Flower to deal three damage to every opposing character. You can achieve this as early as turn three, or weave either version of Max Goof into the sequence somewhere to up the total board wide damage. 

The final nail in the coffin is Milo Thatch - Getting His Hands Dirty, who serves as another potent target for Circle of Life. If you use "Scholar's Gambit" on the turn Milo is reanimated, you guarantee yourself a drawn card from "Practical Knowledge" at the end of the turn. Ward + Bounce is a terrifying combination to handle, especially if you've just had your board annihilated, and it isn't uncommon for Milo to be kept safe by Ward long enough to ferry in a chunk of card advantage. 

The majority of differences between lists at this stage come down to tech choices, but it is worth noting that finalist Nobita was rocking a full four copies of the new Max Goof - Karaoke Star. A shift target that filters away dead songs and quests out incredibly fast? I do wonder if it's good enough to make the cut in future. 

Amber Sapphire Detectives

Amber Sapphire Detectives was beginning to feel like the worst kept secret in Disney Lorcana as DLC Bangkok got closer. There were plenty of doubters that didn't think the deck had what it takes, but if you were in the playtesting trenches you knew ball. 

This archetype has been cooking in the background and has finally reached critical mass with Hyperia City. Somehow, this character-focused aggressive deck is packed with interaction. It can even leverage ink drops to reach all the way to Raging Storm! 

FL-rui's Amber Sapphire Detectives - Top 4 at Disney Lorcana Challenge Bangkok

Yup, that's six different versions of Judy Hopps. What can I say? They breed like rabbits. 

The name of the game here is synergy. In a vacuum, your cards are weaker than your opponents, but as they begin to snowball, they become more than the sum of their parts. This trend started back in Whispers in the Well with Detective-focused payoffs like Judy Hopps - Uncovering Clues and Fangmeyer - Icy Officer, but it's been dialled to eleven with the support in Hyperia City. 

Elisa Maza - Hardworking Detective is disgusting. Sure, the stats are slightly below rate, but this style of targeted discard is the best way to proactively eliminate your opponent's best answers to your slowly snowballing board, all while providing you with perfect information about your opponent's plays. You needed to know if the Prince Phillip combo was in hand? Elisa has you covered. 

It's a similar story for Nick Wilde - Toy Drive Officer, who just does everything that this deck wants to do. Amber Sapphire is uniquely stuffed with big butts to get the best out of Support, while Nick himself rewards you for the selection of cheap characters you already wanted to play with a smooth flow of card draw. Judy Hopps - Day Camp Instructor and Judy Hopps - Always Vigilant are similarly picky about playing a character in the same turn, so your deck is built to make sure it isn't difficult to keep Nick enabled. 

Speaking of, Judy Hopps - Always Vigilant is nasty enough in its own right. Gaston - Superior Archer was already a format-defining piece of interaction, yet Detectives get eight copies of the effect — one of which is cheaper AND searchable! — to lean on. Shift 2 is often backbreaking in making sure that another character has been played, and it isn't uncommon to slam Gaston and Judy in the same turn to completely swing a board that Prince Phillip thought was locked up. 

Detectives wasn't the only way to play Amber Sapphire this weekend either, with the Princess Ramp variant also finding a top eight finish in the hands of an Illumineer named Glenn. As somebody who was already watching the evolution of this deck like a hawk, I'm ecstatic. It's a darn good time to be a fan of yellow and blue, and I cannot recommend that you try out both deck lists any more than I would right now. 

Emerald Steel Midrange

While Jake Quinsee and Joseph Quigley both managed a top eight finish on Emerald Amethyst Retro Evolution Device, it somehow wasn't even the second most-popular recurring villain in the top cut. 

You didn't think Emerald Steel was going to disappear overnight, did you? 

Thiago Santana's Emerald Steel - Top 4 at Disney Lorcana Challenge Bangkok

I said the same thing about Amber Emerald: If it ain't broke...

Thiago Santana's top four list perfectly encapsulates what we've grown to know and love about Emerald Steel: a wall of cheap threats, a dash of resist, and the backbreaking power of Elinor - Renowned Diplomat. If you were unclear about how important Strength of a Raging Fire is to the "curve-out-and-go" Steel deck, we've even got three copies of Max Goof - Rebellious Teen in the deck despite only having one target. 

The biggest innovation here is the movement away from the Darkwing Duck package to facilitate the shiny new pair of two-cost Steel characters from Hyperia City. Flash - Efficient Clerk has a premium stat line with a situational powerful effect that shuts down upcoming players like Mulan - Martial Arts Master.

Toulouse is the real gold standard upgrade though. 'Pete - Games Referee but smaller' is still a format-defining card, and these aggressively slanted decks are the best place for it. Not only is the body worth more, but most opponents are relying on cheap actions to slow you down and allow their card quality to outclass yours. Toulouse shuts those out with ease and can be timed to perfection with the help of Ursula - Deceiver. 

The more that Circle of Life and Mean, Malicious and Scary cement themselves as the benchmarks of the format, the more I find myself wanting to play a Steel deck with Toulouse. If I had a big tournament tomorrow? I think this deck is where I'd be. 

Emerald Ruby Family Photo

Finally, I wanted to chat about the coolest deck that managed to make the Top 16 in Bangkok. There were endless whispers about the potential of Rivera Family Photo and The Torn Corner after they were revealed in Hyperia City, I just hadn't seen the shell come together for them yet. 

I thought it would be another Amber Circle of Life shell, but it seems that Emerald gets the nod because of those infamous Prince Phillip - Vanquisher of Foes combos. 

BTD_Arnold_ pe's Ruby Emerald Family Photo - Top 16 at Disney Lorcana Challenge Bangkok

It might feel more apt to refer to this as Emerald Ruby Actions, given those are the most prominent part of the deck. Emerald Ruby is looking to get a critical mass of cards into the discard to enable gigantic payoffs like Olaf - Snowman of Action and Rivera Family Photo, both of which offer their own engines that make them flourish.

Rivera Family Photo continuously moves two cards from your deck into the discard, which simultaneously fills the discard for Olaf, activates Lyle Tiberius Rourke - Adventurer for Hire and The Leviathan - Guardian of Atlantis on demand, and provides you with a way to cheat The Torn Corner into play. 

Even better, it offers you inevitability. Once you've swept away your opponent's threats, it will slowly and methodically gain you all the lore you need. Between all the board wipes and incidental draw from The Torn Corner, you have a shocking amount of staying power. 

This is also the perfect home for Max Goof - Karaoke Star. You have an excess of songs to discard, it helps activate your discard-focused cards, and it'll regularly quest for four as your discard fills up. It's just a custom card for this archetype and you're never unhappy to see it. 

Another Tale to Spin is a meaningful consistency piece in that regard too, offering you another cheap song that accelerates towards your big The Leviathan - Guardian of Atlantis turn, but can be happily discarded to Max Goof, Tod - Clever Fox or Strike a Good Match once the work is done. 

I also wanted to highlight the really cool synergy between Olaf - Snowman of Action and Retro Evolution Device. Olaf usually costs a minimal number of resources by the time it hits the table, and "Chaotic Collision" should stabilize you as it does. Once you do so, you can cash Olaf out to the Retro Evolution Device to immediately cheat out a Prince Phillip - Vanquisher of Foes or The Leviathan - Guardian of Atlantis. 

This often leads to spots where the opponent thinks they're safe from the whammy when they're absolutely not. It's very sweet and I highly recommend giving it a shake. 

Closing Thoughts

I'm overjoyed to see the Core Constructed format evolving into a mixture of old stalwarts and new blood. That's everything I want from the early events following a set release. Hyperia City has got things looking really sweet and I have no doubt that Disney Lorcana Challenge Bangkok is just the beginning. 

Have further questions? Let me know over at @HowlingMines on X (formerly Twitter) or @howlingmines.com over on Bluesky! Alternatively, give my other work here on TCGplayer a peek if you'd like another slice of everything nice about your favorite game.

But until next time. I've been HowlingMines, you've been amazing!

Stay safe out there — and happy gaming!

The Biggest Price Drops in Pokémon This Week - 11/04/2026

30th Celebration and Ascended Heroes reached new lows this week.

By Corbin Hosler

|@Chosler
|

Published Nov 4, 2026

|

5 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Movers and Shakers

Modern down, vintage and mid era up—it's like the Pokémon TCG market is working backwards.

That's the state of affairs as we officially move into November and the beginnings of what will be a very telling holiday season for the Pokémon market. While store shelves continue to sit empty and big box retailers sell out instantly when they do get product in, sealed prices remain relatively high, at least for the most popular sets like 30th Celebration.

But the singles market has struggled. The market as a whole is of course down over the last several months—offering a discounted opportunity to buy the chase cards you've been eyeing—and 30th Celebration in particular is still dropping as you would expect. The Pokémon Company is doing everything they can to make sure product for this set continues to find its way to shelves.

30th Celebration Singles Get Low

Speaking of discounts, consider this a reminder to myself as much as everyone else that Gengar ex 154 is down this week to a $59 Market Price, the first time it's dipped below $60 since it released back in the middle of September. The current price is only down $5 or so from where it was a month ago but it is still sliding, illustrating that while the downward pressure on 30th Celebrations singles may be abating, it's not done yet.

Likewise, Mew ex is down to its lowest point yet at $65, a drop of $15-20 from where it was a couple of weeks ago and far off the $100 high it held for the first several weeks after release. Night Pikachu dipped to $53 from $60 two weeks ago, and Future Mew has fallen down to $45, from $60 a month ago.

One the cards at least somewhat bucking the trend in the set is Sylveon ex, which this week actually overtook Future Mewtwo in the set's pecking order. Sylveon ex comes in at $39 today, which is essentially the same price it was three weeks ago. As far as anything in the most popular set of all time might be considered a "sleeper," Sylveon is one to keep an eye on.

Amazing Rares Bounce Back

Quick question: do you know what an Amazing Rare is? Yes, that's capital letters there—an "Amazing Rare" in Pokémon TCG parlance is a card printed at a special rarity level they created for the Sword and Shield Series of sets, including the Rayquaza from 2020's Vivid Voltage you see above. The price on this has been all over the place at times during the past year—it went from as low as $13 to as high as $33 back in July, before sliding back down to just over $20.

But it's now climbing again, typical of a card that's just starting to pick up and stop-and-go momentum. Today Rayquaza is back up to a $28 Market Price and Near Mint listings begin at $30.

Rayquaza isn't the only Amazing Rare to start moving in price. Most of them have hung out so far in the $5-10 range, and while nothing has changed there yet, the cycle of Amazing Rares is trending a few dollars higher in almost every case. That includes Jirachi and Celebi from Vivid Voltage, both of which were around $6 but have climbed several dollars higher in the last several weeks. Raikou is another interesting one to keep an eye on, as in the last several weeks it's actually poked up from $5 to closer to $10.

Vintage Sneaks In Wins

Our big vintage representative of the day, Blaine's Charizard is an iconic early Pokémon pull, and the price over the many years since it was printed in Gym Challenge has always reflected that. But while the price on such a behemoth moves slowly, it does move. Blaine's Charizard is up this week from $530 up to a $590 Market Price, reflecting the price movement of just a few individual sales but serving as an effective avatar for the market for chase vintage cards as a whole.

The money in the Pokémon market is always moving somewhere, and this is a perfect example of that after years of chasing after modern pulls.

Another highlight from a mid-era set, this time it's 2015's XY—Ancient Origins. Lugia is very popular in whatever set it's placed in, and this one was no exception. Lugia-EX is up sharply over the last month, climbing up from $215 at the beginning of October all the way up to a $290 Market Price today, an all-time high for the printing.

Ascended Heroes Descends to Earth

Dropping below $200 is the Team Rocket's Mewtwo ex from Ascended Heroes, the set that has established both the highs and lows of the Pokémon market. The set proved to be mega-popular when it dropped and produced several cards worth north of $1,000 as everyone chased Mega Gengar ex.

But that financial destiny wasn't meant to be, at least for now. Instead Ascended Heroes has plummeted in price as reprints have flooded the market, and once again prices on some of the top cards are down this week. That includes Team Rocket's Mewtwo ex, which dropped below $200 for the first time with a precipitous fall from $200 to $180. Joining it on the downward slope is the aforementioned Mega Gengar ex, which is down this week to an all-time low of just $710.

It's up for you to decide whether that's a deal worth snagging or not, but it's the lowest across-the-board prices we've seen on Ascended Heroes, which also has N's Zoroark ex falling from $120 down to under $100 this week for the first time.

With Halloween now behind us, that means Thanksgiving is right around the corner for those in the United States—and, more relevant for this topic, Black Friday. That marks the "official" start of the holiday shopping season, and it's a time when demand is very high and prices could very well follow. If the Pokémon singles market is going to rebound anytime soon, this month could well be the beginning of it. Either way, there's money flowing in the hobby, even if right now a bunch of it is going to cards that were printed before you were born. We'll continue to track the latest developments!

item.title: Clown Crew Advanced Yu-Gi-Oh Deck Guide
item.description:

Clown Crew Advanced Yu-Gi-Oh Deck Guide

No funny business.

By Hanko Chow

|

Published Nov 5, 2026

|

9 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Are you a fan of Monarchs, True Draco, Floowandereeze or just Tribute Summoning in general? Then perhaps you should try the newest Tribute Summoning strategy, Clown Crew! Thanks to its latest support in Beyond The Brave, Clown Crew finally has multiple possible win conditions, a resource management system and a ton of draw power, making it a real top-tier contender.

Clown Crew Yu-Gi-Oh Deck List

This might not be the perfect list since I'm still testing it, but I think 50 cards makes sense to me. I'm already including 18 hand traps and the set of The Great Gallant Bandit as an impactful card going second in the Main Deck and you're sure to see at least one or two copies of the 15 one-card starters in the deck. I highly believe that having all of these possible win condition cards is what makes Clown Crew such a threat at the competitive level so I wouldn't know what to cut if I wanted to.

Clown Crew Key Cards

First, meet your fellow Clowns, starting with Clown Crew Flair! Remember Ame no Habakiri no Mitsurugi? Flair is similar as it helps search for any Clown Crew card as long as you can discard a card after. Already have Clown Crew Biancaviso? Then you'll need Clown Crew Malabarisme. Missing both? Then let's hope that the Clown Crew Rehearsal works out well. Everything usually ends up towards this formation so that Biancaviso can hit the stage with a bang!

Next up we the newest member of the group that really enabled the deck to be a true one-card combo strategy, Clown Crew Cappello. By putting Cappello in your Pendulum Scale, it can put itself onto the field by sending another Clown Crew card from your Deck to the graveyard. All of the Clown Crew Traps have an amazing graveyard effect so you'll usually be sending Clown Crew Finale as this Trap has the effect to search for another by tributing Capello or any other Clown Crew member. Capello when tributed not only shuffles back Pendulums from the field or face-up Extra Deck, but could instead summon another to make sure you still have someone performing on stage for another play.

Clown Crew Flair and Clown Crew Cappello work well together, but the next members also play an important role too. You'll usually prioritize summoning Clown Crew Fiends and Clown Crew Diabolo off Clown Crew Malabarisme, but if you already summoned or used one of them, then Clown Crew Meteor can make a special appearance. Fiends and Diabolo are more important at the start since they also search for more of your end board pieces when Tributed.

Clown Crew Dristy is not a cast member you'll usually summon unless the situation calls for it. Of course, it can shuffle back all Link monsters from the Field or graveyard when tributed which is very important against Link decks, but the other option when tributed is to force both players to shuffle back their hand and redraw the same number. This trick can be useful if you know your opponent just searched for something important, or your hand doesn't have what you need. More importantly, it can combo with Droll & Lock Bird if you time the trigger effects right, allowing you to shuffle away both player's hands after Droll & Lock Bird resolves in the same chain so that neither player can redraw their hand.

Dristy allows your Tribute Summoned monsters to attack twice during the Battle Phase, Fiends boosts your Tribute Summoned monsters ATK by 1000, and Diabolo gives double piercing damage when your Tribute Summoned monsters attack an opponent's Defense mode monster. Cappello can even reduce the DEF points of the opponent's monsters by 1500. You'll realize that there will be game states where you'll want to summon these Clown Crew members beside your Tribute Summoned monster, whether it be Biancaviso or anyone else, as they each help you deal a ton of damage!

Now that you've gotten familiar with the cast and crew behind the scenes, it's time to meet the main star of the show, Clown Crew Biancaviso! It can be Tribute Summoned by using one monster (either Ritual, Fusion, Synchro, Xyz, Pendulum or Link) if you want, but you'll want to Tribute summon it with the normal amount of two for a bigger impact. Biancaviso has an on-tribute-summon effect that either draws cards equal to the number of monsters used for the Tribute Summon or negates face-up cards your opponent controls equal to the number of monsters used for the Tribute Summon. Whether you'll want to draw more cards or negate more cards is something you'll need to figure out every time you summon Biancaviso. Usually you'll want to draw more cards, but there will be times when negating what they have is correct.

On the opponent's turn, Clown Crew Biancaviso puts on a show, allowing you to perform another Tribute Summon of any monster as long as you have the requirements for the Tribute Summon. This ability compliments very well with a copy of Clown Crew Malabarisme or Clown Crew Soiree Operations if you already have another Biancaviso or a Tribute Summon monster in your hand. Luckily, Clown Crew Soiree Operations can either summon two members just like Malabarisme or search for another Clown Crew Monster to your hand. Since the Trap's on-field effect can each be used once per turn, having multiple copies of Clown Crew Soiree Operations makes sense, especially since its graveyard effect allows you to perform an additional Tribute Summon exclusively for a Clown Crew monster, which can create the perfect setup to perform another Tribute Summon for another Biancaviso!

Cappello wasn't the only new member added to the deck. The Great Gallant Bandit is great in this deck, not only as a board breaker but to make sure your Clown Crew Matinee Operatics can resolve during the End Phase to draw all those important hand traps.

As for the other interesting tech options I've included, the "Nouvelles" package of Concours de Cuisine (Culinary Confrontation) and Poissonniere de Nouvelles not only act as another method to search for Clown Crew Flair, but by including Miracle Raven, I've given the deck another option to summon two bodies in case you can't get two Clown Crew members with Clown Crew Malabarisme. Fun fact: you can use Concours de Cuisine (Culinary Confrontation) to deny your Angelechy opponent's Angelechy Opening to e4 by summoning the Patissciel Couverture to their Extra Monster Zone.

Since Clown Crew Malabarisme, Clown Crew Matinee Operatics and Clown Crew Soiree Operations all prevent you from activating monster effects summoned from the Extra Deck until the end of the next turn, There aren't that many viable Extra Deck options aside from possibly Gorgon of Zilofthonia since you can Link climb into a Link-3 pretty easily with Dristy. Underworld Goddess of the Closed World may also be viable if you can control a Dristy and several other monsters. Barricadeborg Blocker is also a neat option as it helps defend from an opponent's Ghost Ogre & Snow Rabbit against your Clown Crew Matinee Operatics. Linkuriboh is very easy to summon since there are several Level 1's in the deck but if you can stick a Clown Crew Flair on the field during your opponent's turn, then having the option to tribute the Flair to reborn the Linkuriboh can be clutch as that will trigger Flair's effect.

All of these Link options are fine to include but you could also just substitute all of them with Fusion monsters you can summon with Super Polymerization. You probably don't need Mudragon of the Swamp since Clown Crew Diabolo has the exact same Fusion Materials, but Garura, Wings of Resonant Life, Elder Entity Norden, Secreterion Dragon, Magistus Chorozo and other Fusions can easily be a better option. That is, unless you really believe in The Great Gallant Bandit or The Winged Dragon of Ra - Sphere Mode.

How to Play Clown Crew

Before Beyond the Brave, Clown Crew suffered from having obvious choke points. A simple Ash Blossom & Joyous Spring or Dominus Impulse against Clown Crew Malabarisme can really prevent you from assembling enough bodies for a valuable Tribute Summon. Ash Blossom or even Ghost Ogre & Snow Rabbit can also deny the draw effect from Clown Crew Matinee Operatics. Well, Clown Crew Cappello can help the strategy get more bodies for Tribute fodder and act as a bait for Ghost Ogre & Snow Rabbit so that Matinee Operatics has better odds of resolving. The Great Gallant Bandit can also beat Ghost Ogre & Snow Rabbit while also acting as a board breaker going second and a decent negate in general. This strategy only had one way of Tribute Summoning per turn, but you can send a copy of Clown Crew Soiree Operations to the graveyard with Cappello or discard it for Clown Crew Flair! The graveyard effect is what the deck needs to make sure it can play with cards like The Great Gallant Bandit or The Winged Dragon of Ra - Sphere Mode.

There are several win conditions in the deck, the main one being Clown Crew Matinee Operatics. The resource swing wins the game nine out of 10 times off of the amount of hand traps you can throw at the opponent to stump their plays alongside the Clown Crew disruptions. The secondary win condition is the combo with Droll & Lock Bird and Clown Crew Flair if you time the trigger effects right. This allows you to shuffle away both player's hands after Droll & Lock Bird resolves in the same chain so that neither player can redraw their hand. It's not very likely, but it can happen from time to time. The last cheeky win condition is Vanity's Ruler. It can easily be found Cyber Angel Benten since you're already using Preparation of Rites to search for Clown Crew Flair. Having the secondary option to search for Cyber Angel Benten is important since Vanity's Ruler itself is just that powerful and it's very easy to "tribute" Cyber Angel Benten off card effects like Clown Crew Rehearsal, Clown Crew Finale and Miracle Raven. Post-side, Cyber Angel Benten can even offer the option to search for Artifact Lancea to really stump decks like Invoked, Angelechy and Maliss.

Will There Be An Encore?

I personally believe that Clown Crew still feels like an incomplete deck. I think if they introduced another "Monarch" into the deck, that it would make the deck's Tribute Summon more impactful going second. It may have all the tools it needs to beat strategies that summon cards from the Extra Deck, Rituals or Pendulums, but it may struggle against any matchup that uses only Normal or plain Effect monsters.

I also think it would be great if there was a new Clown Crew member that includes a continuous protection effect, either to prevent the opponent from targeting Clown Crew cards, or to protect Clown Crew cards from destruction effects. Otherwise, the Clown cards on the field feel very vulnerable to removal effects.

All in all, Clown Crew right now is a competitively viable deck with a simple game plan and many strong setups that can win the game quickly. It already is seeing some competitive success at Regional levels, so I wonder if it has what it takes to be successful at YCS Orlando in this new era of Yu-Gi-Oh!

The Biggest Price Spikes in Magic: The Gathering This Week - 11/05/2026

Goyf is back in Modern (no, not that Goyf).

By Corbin Hosler

|@Chosler
|

Published Nov 5, 2026

|

5 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Movers and Shakers

Is 'Goyf back in Modern?

It sure seems like it is. And while we're fresh off of Eternal Weekend where Andrea Mengucci won the Vintage Championship, let's first start with the return of 'Goyf to the format. And I don't mean Tarmogoyf in Standard, despite it being reprinted into the format recently with Reality Fracture. I'm talking, of course, about the black Goyf, Nethergoyf

As we first touched on last week, this little – well, usually no so little – guy has begun to pop up more and more in Modern, mostly as part of Rakdos Moonshadow but occasionally other places as well. The Magic World Championship for 2026 is next week and will feature Standard, but we'll be back to Modern with the first Pro Tour of 2027, which means more eyes on the rising Nethergoyf.

The Modern Horizons 3 mythic rare climbed in Market Price this week up to over $10 for the first time since shortly after its release back in 2024. That's up from $5 just two weeks ago, and up even more from the $3 it bottomed out at over the summer.

I don't want to dwell too much on Modern this week, because we have a handful of cards climbing in price still from Reality Fracture that we want to cover before Star Trek arrives next week and assuredly takes over the Movers and Shakers for the foreseeable future. Gandalf, White Rider has been a huge winner from the release of Reality Fracture, combining perfectly with Denzilore Fatehold to produce a ton of +1/+1 counters on creatures you control, while also providing them a temporary boost as well. All in all, it produces a lot of power in a hurry, giving the Denzilore player a game-winning Commander endgame.

It sent the price of Gandalf, White Rider skyrocketing. It's up this week to an all-time high Market Price of $9 and climbing, continuing a very steady run that began back as far back as this summer and really picked up steam with Denzilore. Back in July, Gandalf, White Rider actually very briefly dipped below $2, but it's been steady climbing since and climbed to $9 from around $4-5 just a month ago.

The Theorist, Jace Beleren has brought back some attention to the first planeswalker to come with a combination of words that allowed cards to be drawn on an opponent's turn. Teferi, Master of Time can't compete with The Theorist for obvious reasons, but it can certainly play extremely well alongside him. The extra attention has caused Teferi, Master of Time's price to slowly start to tick up, and this week it climbed up to an all-time high of $14, up from $7-8 just two months ago.

I'm not positive exactly what's causing the climb on this; I suspect it may be nothing in particular and more the fact that Valgavoth, Harrower of Souls is just a powerhouse. For four mana, you get a 4/4 that has an incredible set of Commander abilities. While the ward cost is not overly problematic to play, it does naturally trigger Valgavoth's second ability if they have to target it at sorcery speed. Plus, it's pretty common for Valgavoth's second ability to get triggered at least one time in a turn cycle, without even going into cards that you can play alongside Valgavoth to ensure it hits.

It's also quickly approaching an all-time high at $25, continuing a climb that really began as far back as January 2026. That's when Valgavoth was selling for around $9. By May, it had reached $15. By August, $20. And today it's going for around $25 a copy, with no other printings of this Valgavoth out there.

How about a little Valgavoth two-for-one? The headliner of Duskmourn: House of Horror is about to rotate out of Standard, where it saw little play, but the price is going the opposite direction of what you expect from a rotating card. Instead, Valgavoth, Terror Eater has climbed in Market Price from $16 a month ago up to almost $25 today, easily a post-release all-time for the card (for what it's worth, the Showcase printing's price has moved in lockstep with its main set counterpart). Valgavoth is one of the better reanimation targets even in 2026, and that has helped to push the price higher than anyone might expect for a Standard-legal mythic rare that's not really all that heavily played in the format.

Moving on to Marvel Super Heroes, here's a bit of a surprising one. The Loki-flavored skin of Spark Double has lagged behind its counterpart in price ever since its printing, honestly likely owing to the fact that the alternately named card won't come up as much in algorithmic sales platforms. But players did catch on that at one point earlier this year Loki's Double was going for half the price of a regular Spark Double.

That's changed today, and Loki's Double is now climbing quickly to catch the rest of its printings at the $12 mark. For now, it is up to almost $10 in Market Price, climbing from the $5 it was just a month ago.

Avacyn, Angel of Horror from Commander: Reality Fracture seems to be the biggest user of The Darkness Crystal, along with a lot of other decks in Commander. While the FINAL FANTASY artifact hasn't made its way into 60-card formats yet, it works well enough in Commander including in all the new Avacyn decks being built. As a result, the price on this Rare climbed from $4 just two weeks ago up to almost $8 today.

Finally this week, let's go back. Back to 2005, when Betrayers of Kamigawa released with Lifegift printed at rare. A precursor of the now-ubiquitous landfall mechanic, the one-mana enchantment languished as a dollar rare for most of its existence. It eventually found a reason to jump in price back in 2021, and ultimately settled in around $7-8 after that.

But Lifegift is once again on the upswing, and as a result of there simply being so little inventory of a 20-plus years-old set, Lifegift has spiked very hard since the release of Reality Fracture and Kwia Vigorbloom. It's up this week officially to a $24 Market Price, but live listings are actually closer to the $35 range right now. It's a heck of a three-drop from Betrayers of Kamigawa!

Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek Limited Set Review: White

It seems highly illogical to play white, Martin explains why.

By Martin Jůza

|@MartinJuza
|

Published Nov 5, 2026

|

17 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Welcome to the Set Reviews for Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek! We're directing all auxiliary power to Limited Expertise as myself, Reid Duke, and Luis Scott-Vargas will be preparing you for Prerelease and your first booster draft. We'll cover every single card that you can open in a Star Trek Play Booster, including the 30 Stardates bonus cards, which will be included with their respective colors.

Understanding what you can open is important for Limited, so here's the Play Booster spread for Star Trek:

  • 7 Commons, with one replaced by a Stardates card in 1 out of 25 boosters
  • 3 Uncommon
  • 1 Rare or mythic rare
  • 1 Wildcard of any rarity
  • 1 Traditional foil card of any rarity
  • 1 Non-foil or traditional foil land. Either a basic or common dual land with 50% likelihood of each

That's 14 playable cards, plus one double-sided token. Unlike Reality Fracture, there's no weird collation with treatments or paired cards this time around. It should feel more familiar if you're someone who plays a lot of Limited. Let's look at the ten archetypes you can play in Star Trek as published by Wizards of the Coast:

Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek Limited Grading Scale

  • Read More: How to Build a Prerelease Deck In Magic: The Gathering

Before I dive into the cards, let's talk about the grading process. Our Limited grading scale is designed to give you a sense of how cards compare to one another, but the grade is less informative than the commentary, so use both to evaluate cards. We use a 0-5 scale for our Set Reviews, with good commons usually landing around 3.0-3.5 and good rares 4.0 and higher. Here's the scale for Star Trek:

  • 5.0: The best of the best, the most powerful cards in the set (such as The Theorist, Jace Beleren or Ajani Unrelenting)
  • 4.5: Incredible Limited card, but just shy of the literal best cards in the set (such as Austere Command or Chandra, Torch of Defiance)
  • 3.5: Top-tier common or good uncommon (Rewrite Regrets)
  • 3.0: You basically never cut these (Protege's Awakening)
  • 2.5: Solid playable that rarely gets cut (Teyo, Lightshield Expert)
  • 2.0: Decent filler, but sometimes gets cut (Rank Rat)
  • 1.5: Pure card filler, which you cut most of the time (Fateshaper Aspirant)
  • 1.0: Bad filler, which you cut almost all the time (Yargle, Glutton of Urborg)
  • 0.0: Completely unplayable under all circumstances (Loyal Tutor)

Where to Find Star Trek Limited Set Reviews

  • Star Trek Limited Set Review: Blue
  • Star Trek Limited Set Review: Black
  • Star Trek Limited Set Review: Green
  • Star Trek Limited Set Review: Gold, Colorless, and Lands

Limited: 3.25

 

Two mana to exile any creature or Spacecraft is an amazing deal, but giving your opponent a free land is a real drawback, especially early in the game or if your opponent is on a three-color deck. Try to wait for a high value target later in the game when the extra land is much less likely to be relevant.

First Copy: 0.1 / Second Copy: 1.25 / Third+ Copy: 2.0

 

3/1 for three is a pretty bad deal, especially in a format full of 1/1 tokens and other playable one mana creatures that can easily trade for Andromedan Automatons. I'd need to have at least three copies in a regular deck to consider running these, or two in a deck with some very powerful artifact synergies. Getting an extra copy or two doesn't change the fact that it is still a bad creature.

Limited: 4.25

 

A two-mana 2/3 that can start producing creatures as early as turn three is an amazing card that will shine especially brightest in the White/Black archetype which revolves around artifacts. The ability applies to Incorporator itself, so it doesn't even need any extra support.

Limited: 2.0 - 3.0

 

Two bodies for two mana is a solid baseline, and both being artifact creatures matters quite a bit in this format. Assembly Specialist is going to be the best fit in White/Black artifact decks, but can be useful in other decks as well that are utilizing cheap equipment or going wide. Good synergy with beam me up cards as well to create more value. Assembly Specialist can range from mediocre to solid depending on your deck, but there are enough ways to make them useful in this format that it should be a good card.

Limited: 4.5

 

Speaking of payoff cards for decks that are trying to go wide, [Benny Russell, Dreamer (Mikaeus, the Lunarch)(product-hover id="726790") is one of the very best. Flexible mana cost, good early and late, along with being very splashable. Lots of playable one-drops in this format improves the power of this card even more. That said, this should be one of the best cards in the set.

Limited: 3.0

 

A two-mana 2/2 with lifelink is already a reasonable card. Brad synergizes well with Spacecrafts where his ability resolves before the station ability, so he adds three counters instead of two. There are also plenty of creatures with +1/+1 counters and cards like Pure Energy and Shields Up!. Brad should be quite good in White/Green and White/Blue and reasonable elsewhere.

In White/Blue: 4.0
Elsewhere: 2.5

 

I would mostly ignore the five-color activation of Captain Benjamin Sisko and evaluate him based on how often your deck can face a dilemma. This should be trivial mostly in the White/Blue archetype, where this mechanic is the name of the game. Don't let the rare symbol fool you into thinking this should always be a high pick though, as the 2/2 body without any form of evasion is not particularly exciting for Limited.

Limited: 5.0

 

This card is incredible. It's a creature-producing value engine that also boosts your board and can even fetch a Spacecraft from your deck directly onto the battlefield if the game goes long enough. If your opponent doesn't have an immediate answer, they are going to be in a lot of trouble.

Sealed: 3.0
Draft: 2.5

 

Solid filler that triggers your dilemma cards, but awkward against Spacecrafts against which you have to take the hit at least once. Usually quite reliable in Sealed where I would almost never cut it. Board it out in Traditional Draft if you are playing a matchup where spending two mana to replace a card is too big of a momentum loss.

Limited: 2.0

 

Normally I would be happy to run Savannah Lions in any white deck, but this format features so many 1/1 tokens and cards like Assembly Specialist that I am not quite sure if this should always be an automatic inclusion. Being an artifact is a nice upside for White/Black decks, but one toughness could be too big of a drawback in certain matchups.

Limited: 0.0 - 3.0

 

Conquest Mission is a build-around card for dedicated White/Black artifact decks where it can range from slow to great depending on your build. Taking your third turn off to play a card that doesn't immediately impact the board can be quite costly, so you will need plenty of cheap artifacts to make up for the loss of momentum and also something to take advantage of the artifact tokens.

Limited: 4.5

 

Deanna Troi is a great value engine and the only requirement is to play more creatures. Potentially a game winning card on turn two if your opponent doesn't have an immediate answer. Cheap in mana cost, works great with tokens, synergizes with +1/+1 counters. Great card.

Limited: 1.25

 

Mediocre filler with a small upside of being an artifact.

Limited:0.5 - 3.0

 

Dr. Beverly Crusher doubles her own lifegain trigger, so any life gained converts into two +1/+1 counters. That's a solid payoff for repeatable lifegain, albeit a bit slow. I can imagine she could become even better in some of the multicolor decks taking full advantage of strange new worlds by running a lot of the Gain Lands, in addition to some other ways of repeatedly gaining life with lifelinking creatures or cards like Obsidian Order Operative. That said, the mythic symbol is likely a bit misleading here as I don't see enough ways to consistently trigger her to make me want to take this highly.

Limited: 3.5

 

The total stats are below rate, but the protection ability is very strong. This format features a ton of creatures that come with a +1/+1 counter and other ways to put them on your creatures like Pure Energy and Shields Up!. Keep in mind that the effect removes all the +1/+1 counters from the creature, so a creature with three counters doesn't get to survive being destroyed three times.

Limited: 1.0 - 2.5

 

A one-mana 1/2 that gains one life isn't very exciting by itself, but both effects support several different white strategies, including being an artifact creature in White/Black, adding a +1/+1 counter in White/Green and giving you a cheap creature for the beam me up mechanic. You shouldn't fill your deck with these just because they cost one mana, but the first copy can be quite useful in a lot of decks in this format.

Limited: 4.5

 

Excalbian Gamemaster seems incredible for Sealed, where I expect the three-color green decks to be very popular. Great against removal and easy enough to splash. Cards like this are great reasons to look out for a dual land here and there throughout the draft, as it both enables splashes and also to have more lands with different names, even if you aren't playing more than two colors.

Limited: 1.5

 

Filler level material with the upside of being flexible and supporting a few different archetypes. That said, neither of the modes is particularly exciting, as four mana for 4/3 vigilance or a 3/2 creature that draws a card is not something you would want to run in your deck these days.

Limited: 0.5

 

Tutor effects are generally quite bad in Limited because the loss of tempo is usually too costly. I don't see any Auras or Equipment worth the trouble of paying two more mana for and if you are going to find a Spacecraft with this, the tempo loss is going to be even bigger since you are not adding anything to the board in the meantime.

Limited: 0.25

 

There are two types of players. One sees Flare of Fortitude and immediately imagines the perfect scenario where after a long board stall, your opponent attacks with everything, you block and use this card to remove all of their creatures while granting yours with indestructible. The other player is me, who instead pictures all the moments where any proactive card would help me close out the game, but instead I have a glorified Fog rotting in my hand for the entire game. In turn, this gives my opponent just enough time to turn the game around. This card is too costly and too situational to consider playing.

Limited: 2.5

 

Land cyclers are always at least good fillers, and sometimes even better if you are splashing or in this case if your deck is going wide. Being an artifact is also an upside here.

Limited: 5.0

 

Given the nature of this format with expensive Spacecrafts and the strange new worlds mechanic, I am fully expecting the games to be quite slow, especially at Prerelease. You should have plenty of time to fix your mana and find your splashes and get your expensive cards online. This is one of those cards that can completely take over and win the game by itself. Make sure you add as many dual lands as possible to take full advantage of all the abilities.

Limited: 3.5

 

I like this card quite a bit. The stats are not that exciting, but evasion combined with utility makes this a good card. Synergizes well with creatures with good "enter the battlefield" effects, saves your creatures from aura-based removal while providing a reasonable threat that's a great target for +1/+1 counters.

Limited: 4.0

 

Hologram Janeway seems quite good to me. A regular curve of two, three and four-drop creatures should comfortably get you a +1/+1 trigger on turn four that will also make it easier to attack profitably. Remember that you don't need to have a total of eight power of attacking creatures, just eight power total.

Limited: 0.5 - 3.0

 

Kirk has a very poor baseline and will take a lot of work and a perfect mana base to take full advantage of. That said, 104 of the 306 cards in this set have a legendary subtype, 61 of which cost three or less mana. Even just one more legendary card of a different color, you should have multiple cards in your deck to search for. There might be a very specific strange new worlds deck where Kirk could actively be good, but I wouldn't expect that to happen often. Unlike General Picard, this isn't a card I would make an adjustment for.

Limited: 3.5

 

Evergreen white removal spell that has the upside of exiling any non-land permanent and downside of being susceptible to effects that destroy an artifact, although ward helps quite a bit here. Easily splashable.

Sealed: 1.5 - 2.0
Draft: 2.5

 

Using this card as removal only works for two turns so you have a very limited window to capitalize on it. Using it for value by targeting your own creature with a good "enter the battlefield" effect means you give up way too much momentum. The fact that it effectively replaces itself thanks to the Clue token is what makes this card interesting for aggressive decks, where temporarily removing a blocker can enable good attacks.

Limited: 3.5

 

Miles has a reasonable floor of a three mana 3/3, so the question is how often can you expect to be able and want to return a creature or artifact into your own hand. I can definitely imagine decks with multiple copies of Emergency Medical Hologram, multiple beam me up cards like Pure Energy or simply using it as a way to save your creature from an aura-based removal. It also works well with Tea, Earl Grey, Hot.

Limited: 2.0

 

The Needs of the Many seems like a more useful version of Flare of Fortitude, because of the cheaper cost and ability to sacrifice tokens. This makes it a reasonable combat trick that can effectively counter a removal spell or help you win a fight in combat. Still, I much prefer cards that can be used proactively.

Limited: 3.0

 

Very solid value card that will smooth out your draws and provide a reasonable threat later.

Limited: 0.5 - 2.0

 

This is a tough card to evaluate without playing the format first. The most likely scenario is that this card is just too slow. Investing your entire fourth turn into something that doesn't impact the board is a massive loss in pacing that can easily cost you the game. That said, Spacecrafts indicate that the format could be more on the slower side and I can definitely imagine a defensive deck where this can be a legitimate win condition, especially in Sealed.

Limited: 2.5

 

Pet Sehlat is not the most reliable attacker, but it is great at blocking and stationing Spacecrafts.

Limited: 4.0

 

Picard looks amazing. There are lots of ways to increase his power and a good amount of creatures with evasion to buff with his ability. A great two-drop.

White/Black: 4.25
Elsewhere: 3.25

 

Primary Unimatrix Adjunct gives itself double strike, so the baseline is already reasonable for a four-drop. In a dedicated artifact deck, giving your entire team double strike is going to make combat extremely difficult for your opponent, especially as white has a lot of ways to grow creatures with +1/+1 counters.

White/Green: 3.0
Elsewhere: 2.0

 

Another card where the value mostly depends on the speed of the format and the way it plays out. I expect Pure Energy to be decent in White-Green which cares about +1/+1 counters, but not something you should always play in other combinations.

Limited: 3.0

 

Great value card for any deck running a couple of Spacecrafts and artifacts. With cards like Ghost of Illyria, Miles O'Brien and the beam me up mechanic, good creatures with "enters the battlefield" effects should be quite valuable in this format.

Prerelease: 2.75
Draft: 2.0

 

This is the type of card I will usually play at the Prerelease, but a week or two later once everyone gets some games in with the new cards, Saavik will become extremely telegraphed. The 2/2 body is also very unexciting. The appeal here is that you can (in theory) reuse Saavik with the beam me up mechanic, but that seems really slow.

Limited: 2.5

 

Cheap conditional removal that isn't very exciting when you need to deal with a creature that isn't attacking. The upside is that you face a dilemma which has additional benefits. I am not too thrilled about this card.  

Limited: 2.75

 

Cards like Take Up the Shield have been very solid tricks in the last couple of years and I expect this set to follow suit.

Limited: 1.25

 

Pure filler which you will cut most of the time.

Limited: 3.75

 

A 2/2 with first strike is a very solid baseline, especially in a format where white can easily boost creatures with +1/+1 counters. There are only a handful of equipment cards in the format and you don't want to overload your deck with Spacecrafts, so I would expect to draw more than one card per game with it on average, which is still a very good deal.

Limited: 2.0

 

A filler two-drop that shouldn't be too difficult to trigger, the only problem is that even if you get the +1/+1 counter, it still just trades with other creatures with two power. Nothing to write home about.

Limited: 3.5

 

Putting a +1/+1 counter on each creature you control for two mana is a great deal, especially in a format with a lot of ways to create tokens. It also presents a dilemma and the second mode can be useful as well if you need to make your land drops. I like this card quite a bit.

Limited: 2.0 - 2.5

 

This card seems decent for synergy decks to look for your missing pieces, but a bit too slow for aggressive decks trying to curve out.

Limited: 0.0

 

Troubling Tribbles multiplies relatively fast, but the floor on this card is essentially a blank, so you are going to need to have an extremely good payoff card to take advantage of it. Other than multiple static ways to boost your creatures or a powerful sacrifice outlet, I can't really think of much.

Limited: 2.5

 

This looks like a decent curve-topper that already supplies half the power necessary to trigger it. Goes up in value if your deck features creatures with evasion or lifelink.

Limited: 4.75

 

Creating three tokens immediately makes this much more appealing than a Spacecraft that needs several turns before doing anything. The tokens alone can station it the very next turn and a 5/5 flyer with lifelink and ward should help you stabilize, and then take over most games very quickly.

Sealed: 3.0
Draft: 2.25

 

U.S.S. Excelsior takes quite a while to get online, but comes with a built in removal spell to help you stabilize. You don't usually cut cards like this from your Sealed decks, but I can see this being too slow for draft.

Limited: 2.0

 

Filler two-drop with some extra utility thanks to synergy with the beam me up mechanic. Being an artifact gives it a few extra percentage points in White/Black.

Top 5 White Limited Commons From Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek

  1. Malfunctioning Holodeck
  2. Oberth-Class Starship
  3. Shields Up!
  4. Command Decision
  5. Free Borg Revolutionaries

White does not seem very exciting to me. The commons feel relatively weak, but maybe the whole set feels underpowered to allow pacing to develop Spacecrafts.

The 10 Cards Everybody Wants from Delta Reign

Rayquaza reigns supreme.

By Peter Day

|

Published Oct 29, 2026

|

7 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: The Cards Everybody Wants

The king returns! After more than a decade, Mega Rayquaza is finally coming back to the Pokémon TCG in the November 6 expansion Delta Reign.

Compared to headliners like Charizard, Rayquaza makes far fewer appearances in the Pokémon TCG, but it always leaves a huge impact. The last time we got Mega Rayquaza in cardboard form was back in the 2015 set Ancient Origins, where M Rayquaza-EX quickly became one of the most valuable cards in the Series. Rayquaza later came back in 2020's Evolving Skies, the set that defined the Sword & Shield era and the pandemic-fueled Poké-boom.

So, yeah. Collectors can't wait to open Mega Rayquaza ex, and players are nearly as excited by the prospect of unleashing its Storm Emeralda attack that can KO anything in the game.

That said, Rayquaza isn't the only beloved Pokémon getting rare, strong, and beautiful new cards in Delta Reign. As you're tearing through packs in November, keep an eye out for these heralds of the Sky-High Pokémon's majesty. These are the Pokémon cards everybody wants from Delta Reign.

#10 SIR Mega Golisopod ex

Special Illustration Rare (SIR) is traditionally the most sought-after rarity in modern Pokémon sets, and Delta Reign will be no exception. While SIR Mega Golisopod ex might not be anyone's first pick at this rarity, the challenge of finding it and nagimiso's intense artwork will still make it an exciting pull.

Mega Golisopod ex also threatens a respectable 220 damage for just one Energy as long as the opponent's Active Pokémon already has damage on it. That high single-target damage pairs well with fellow Grass-type Arboliva ex, and could make Golisopod a real contender once Dragapult ex and Teal Mask Ogerpon ex rotate out of Standard in April 2027.

#9 Legendary Pyroduct

Delta Reign introduces a new mechanic to the Pokémon TCG: Legendary Stadiums.

Like Pokémon LEGEND from the HeartGold & SoulSilver Series, these Stadiums are so powerful they're split across two cards, which you have to draw and play together. The resulting Legendary Stadium still gets bumped by your opponent playing a regular Stadium, but as long as it stays in play, it can completely define a game.

Of the three Legendary Stadiums in Delta Reign, the one that players and collectors are most excited for is Legendary Pyroduct. This Stadium shuts down all Abilities on Evolution Pokémon, from Drakloak's Recon Directive to Dudunsparce's Run Away Draw to N's Zoroark ex's Trade and Dusknoir's Cursed Blast. Basic Pokémon remain unaffected, so Legendary Pyroduct slots easily into Basic Box decks, which got another helpful upgrade in Delta Reign we'll cover in #7.

Power aside, this connected artwork pair looks simply gorgeous. The magma that pours through this scene has a delightfully gloopy quality, like you're peering into a red-hot honeycomb, and I love how deftly akagi has integrated the Poké Ball symbol.

#8 IR Growlithe

This Illustration Rare (IR) is here for exactly one reason: it's really, really cute.

Many Pokémon artists have created memorable cards lately by drawing Pokémon doing the same things we're used to seeing our pets do. And it's hard to imagine more adorable pet-like behavior than waiting by the door for you to come home.

#7 Talonflame ex

Talonflame ex may be a Stage 2, but it's going straight into every Basic Box deck as soon as possible—and really, any deck that runs Mega Kangaskhan ex. That's because its Excited Dive lets you drop it onto your Bench as long as you have a Colorless Mega Evolution Pokémon ex in play.

Talonflame and Kangaskhan make a mean tag-team, with both Pokémon hitting hard, drawing or searching cards, and retreating into each other for free (as long as you have Latias ex). The shell around them can and will change as Standard evolves, but this combo will probably define at least one deck during their time in the format. 

Note that Legendary Pyroduct does not shut off Excited Dive, because Excited Dive activates while Talonflame ex is still in your hand. Block evolution decks all you want!

#6 IR Kecleon

Tomokazu Komiya's cards always make me do a double-take.

Besides being trippy and fascinating, Komiya cards have a history of being bought out by speculators. The reasonable assumption is that if a card is memorable, that also makes it desirable.

I don't know if anyone will try to target Kecleon, especially in the current market where vintage is king again and modern chase cards have been dropping across the board. Regardless, Komiya fans will be celebrating come November.

#5 SIR Zinnia's Trust

Wherever Rayquaza goes, Zinnia follows.

Zinnia cards were a big draw in previous Dragon-themed sets like Evolving Skies and Dragon Majesty, and this one will likely continue that trend in Delta Reign—especially given its Special Illustration Rare rarity.

Zinnia also works wonders with the Talonflame ex/Mega Kangaskhan ex duo mentioned above. With Mega Kangaskhan in the Active Spot and Ignition Energy attached, you can swap to Talonflame ex and move the Ignition Energy so you can attack immediately. Then you search up another Zinnia's Trust, so you can keep swapping to whichever Pokémon is less damaged while maintaining your pressure and draw power.

#4 IR Eevee

Count us lucky we got this Eevee in Delta Rein! Over in Japan, it was only available in the Eevee ex Starter Set, which has made it much harder to track down. That context will make dedicated collectors even more hungry for the English version.

Plus, you know… it's Eevee. Riding in a bag. That alone puts it in contention for the most valuable Illustration Rare in the set.

#3 SIR Raikou ex

The Legendary Beasts are still one of the most iconic and beloved Legendary trios in Pokémon history, and Raikou ex will be a must-have Special Illustration Rare for fans of this lightning-fast Pokémon.

Raikou has been underserved in terms of full-art cards in the past, so this dynamic take on the Thunder Pokémon by Oku will immediately flash to the top of the list of the best illustrations it's ever received.

#2 IR Groudon and Promo Kyogre

Speaking of iconic trios, Rayquaza has two counterparts of its own to contend with—the other two points in the triangle that put the "delta" in Delta Reign.

Groudon has returned to the Pokémon TCG, this time as an Illustration Rare. Normally that would put these cards below Special Illustration Rares in terms of desirability, but Ryota Murayama's color-saturated artwork demands too much respect for collectors to overlook.

Its counterpart, Kyogre, isn't technically part of Delta Reign. Instead, this IR-style card is a promo that's only available in Delta Reign Elite Trainer Boxes (either the normal ones, or the Pokémon Center-exclusive ones).

Kyogre and Groudon have a long history of appearing in valuable, mirrored-artwork cards. Regardless of their printed rarity, these are two cards that no collectors will want to move on from Delta Reign without.

#1 MHR and SIR Mega Rayquaza ex

Above every other chase card in Delta Reign is the Sky-High Pokémon itself, Mega Rayquaza.

Mega Rayquaza first appeared in the Pokémon TCG more than a decade ago in Roaring Skies and Ancient Origins, the latter of which gave us one of the most expensive Rayquaza cards ever printed. Now Mega Rayquaza is back with three different versions in Delta Reign, two of which will be the rarest and most valuable cards in the set.

Mega Hyper Rare (MHR) Mega Rayquaza ex is the highest-rarity card in Delta Reign, but you probably could have figured that out just by looking at it. With its gold monochrome finish, this card practically screams "premium," and its Japanese version has a price point to match.

On the other hand, Special Illustration Rare Mega Rayquaza ex brings more colors to bear, making this illustration by Kazuki Minami feel even more intense. Given the precedent set by other Mega Evolution Series sets like Perfect Order, Chaos Rising and Pitch Black, SIR Mega Rayquaza ex will likely rise to become the most expensive card in Delta Reign as more collectors scramble to find this exclusive artwork.
